questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int x^6\,dx\)
questions.explanation:
Using \(\int x^n\,dx = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\) with \(n=6\), the new power is 7 and it must be divided by 7.

This gives \(\dfrac{x^7}{7}+C\), and the constant \(C\) must always be included for an indefinite integral.

questions.explanation:

questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int (e^x + 3)\,dx\)
questions.explanation:
By linearity, \(\int (e^x+3)\,dx = \int e^x\,dx + \int 3\,dx\).

\(\int e^x\,dx = e^x\), and a plain constant integrates as \(\int 3\,dx = 3x\) (not 3 itself).

Adding these and the constant of integration gives \(e^x + 3x + C\).

This is the standard form \(\int \dfrac{du}{\sqrt{a^2-u^2}}=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{u}{a}\right)+C\) with \(u=x-2, a=2\), giving \(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x-2}{2}\right)+C\).
questions.hint: Complete the square under the root first.

questions.topic: Integration as the Inverse Process of Differentiation: Standard Integrals
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^2-4}{x-2}\,dx\)
questions.explanation:
Factor: \(\dfrac{x^2-4}{x-2} = \dfrac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2} = x+2\) (the factors cancel completely).

So \(\int(x+2)dx = \dfrac{x^2}{2}+2x+C\).
questions.hint: Factor the numerator as a difference of squares first — it may cancel with the denominator.

questions.topic: Integration by Substitution and Trigonometric/Algebraic Standard Forms
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int x\sin(2x+3)\,dx\)
questions.explanation:
With \(u=x,\ dv=\sin(2x+3)dx\) so \(v=-\dfrac{\cos(2x+3)}{2}\): \(\int x\sin(2x+3)dx = -\dfrac{x\cos(2x+3)}{2}+\int\dfrac{\cos(2x+3)}{2}dx\).

The leftover integral is \(\dfrac{\sin(2x+3)}{4}\), giving \(-\dfrac{x\cos(2x+3)}{2}+\dfrac{\sin(2x+3)}{4}+C\).
questions.hint: By parts with \(u=x\); the inner argument \(2x+3\) needs the chain rule throughout.
distractor_logic: Reverses the sign on the second term of the by-parts result
Loses the leading \(\frac{1}{2}\) that comes from \(dv=\sin(2x+3)dx\)
Correct antiderivative but the constant of integration is missing

questions.topic: Integration by Partial Fractions
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{x\,dx}{(x+1)(x+2)}\)
questions.explanation:
Decompose: \(\dfrac{x}{(x+1)(x+2)} = \dfrac{-1}{x+1}+\dfrac{2}{x+2}\), so \(F(x)=\log\left|\dfrac{(x+2)^2}{x+1}\right|\).

So \(\int_0^1\dfrac{x\,dx}{(x+1)(x+2)} = \left(\log 9-\log 2\right)-\left(\log 4-\log 1\right) = \log\dfrac{9}{2}-\log 4 = \log\dfrac{9}{8}\).
questions.hint: Decompose into partial fractions first, then evaluate \(F(1)-F(0)\) using log rules.
distractor_logic: Evaluates \(F(0)-F(1)\) instead of \(F(1)-F(0)\), reversing the bounds
Appends a constant of integration, which a definite integral's numeric value never carries
Flips the fraction inside the final logarithm

questions.topic: Integration as the Inverse Process of Differentiation: Standard Integrals
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^3+x}{x^2+1}\,dx\)
questions.explanation:
Factor the numerator: \(x^3+x = x(x^2+1)\), so \(\dfrac{x^3+x}{x^2+1} = x\) — the fraction simplifies completely before any integration technique is needed.

So \(\int x\,dx = \dfrac{x^2}{2}+C\).
questions.hint: Always check whether the numerator factors and cancels with the denominator before reaching for substitution or partial fractions.
distractor_logic: Fails to spot that the fraction cancels completely, and instead splits off a spurious logarithmic piece
Uses the wrong power-rule coefficient on the quadratic term
Correct antiderivative but the constant of integration is missing

questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x\,dx}{(x+1)^2}\)
questions.explanation:
Write \(x=(x+1)-1\), so \(\dfrac{x}{(x+1)^2} = \dfrac{1}{x+1}-\dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2}\).

Integrating: \(\log|x+1|+\dfrac{1}{x+1}+C\).

questions.topic: Integration as the Inverse Process of Differentiation: Standard Integrals
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \sin^3 x\,dx\)
questions.explanation:
Write \(\sin^3x = \sin x(1-\cos^2x)\), then substitute \(t=\cos x,\ dt=-\sin x\,dx\): \(\int\sin x(1-\cos^2x)dx = -\int(1-t^2)dt\).

This gives \(-t+\dfrac{t^3}{3}+C = -\cos x+\dfrac{\cos^3x}{3}+C\).
questions.hint: Peel off one factor of \(\sin x\) to pair with \(dx\), then substitute \(t=\cos x\) for the rest.
distractor_logic: Reverses the sign on the second term after substitution
Reverses the sign on the first term

questions.topic: Integration by Parts
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int (x^2+1)e^x\,dx\)
questions.explanation:
Split: \(\int(x^2+1)e^x\,dx = \int x^2e^x\,dx+\int e^x\,dx\).

Using the Level-2 result \(\int x^2e^x\,dx=e^x(x^2-2x+2)\) and adding \(e^x\): \(e^x(x^2-2x+2)+e^x+C = e^x(x^2-2x+3)+C\).
questions.hint: Split the integrand and reuse the earlier by-parts result for \(\int x^2e^x\,dx\).

Introduces a sign error on only the constant term
Correct antiderivative but the constant of integration is missing

questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\sec x\tan x}{1+\sec x}\,dx\)
questions.explanation:
The antiderivative is \(F(x)=\log(1+\sec x)\) (since the numerator is the derivative of the denominator).

So \(\int_0^{\pi/3}\dfrac{\sec x\tan x}{1+\sec x}dx = \log 3-\log 2 = \log\dfrac{3}{2}\).
questions.hint: Recognize the numerator as the derivative of the denominator: \(\int\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}dx=\log|f(x)|\).
distractor_logic: Evaluates \(F(0)-F(\pi/3)\) instead of \(F(\pi/3)-F(0)\), reversing the bounds

Flips the fraction inside the final logarithm

questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^2+x+1}{x(x+1)}\,dx\)
questions.explanation:
Divide first: \(\dfrac{x^2+x+1}{x(x+1)} = 1+\dfrac{1}{x(x+1)}\), then decompose \(\dfrac{1}{x(x+1)} = \dfrac{1}{x}-\dfrac{1}{x+1}\).

Integrating the whole expression: \(x+\log|x|-\log|x+1|+C\).
questions.hint: Long-divide first (numerator and denominator have the same degree), then apply partial fractions to the remainder.

questions.topic: Integration by Parts
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 x^2 e^{-x}\,dx\)
questions.explanation:
The antiderivative (Level-2 by-parts result) is \(F(x)=-e^{-x}(x^2+2x+2)\). So \(F(1)=-\dfrac{5}{e}\) and \(F(0)=-2\).

Hence \(\int_0^1x^2e^{-x}dx = F(1)-F(0) = -\dfrac{5}{e}-(-2) = 2-\dfrac{5}{e}\).
questions.hint: Use \(\int x^2e^{-x}\,dx=-e^{-x}(x^2+2x+2)\) (a Level-2 by-parts result), then substitute the limits.

Appends a constant of integration, which a definite integral's numeric value never carries
Introduces a sign error when substituting the upper limit into the by-parts antiderivative

questions.topic: Integration by Partial Fractions
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{dx}{x^2+7x+10}\)
questions.explanation:
Since \(x^2+7x+10=(x+2)(x+5)\), the antiderivative is \(F(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}\log\left|\dfrac{x+2}{x+5}\right|\).

So \(\int_0^1\dfrac{dx}{x^2+7x+10} = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\log\dfrac{3}{6}-\log\dfrac{2}{5}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}\log\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{5}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}\log\dfrac{5}{4}\).
questions.hint: Factor the denominator, decompose into partial fractions, then evaluate \(F(1)-F(0)\).

questions.topic: Integration by Parts
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} x^2\cos x\,dx\)
questions.explanation:
The antiderivative (Level-2 by-parts result) is \(F(x)=x^2\sin x+2x\cos x-2\sin x\). At \(x=\pi/2\): \(F(\pi/2)=\dfrac{\pi^2}{4}+0-2 = \dfrac{\pi^2}{4}-2\), and \(F(0)=0\).

Hence \(\int_0^{\pi/2}x^2\cos x\,dx = \dfrac{\pi^2}{4}-2\).
questions.hint: Use \(\int x^2\cos x\,dx=x^2\sin x+2x\cos x-2\sin x\) (a Level-2 by-parts result), then substitute the limits carefully.

Introduces a sign error on the last term while substituting the upper limit

questions.topic: Integration by Substitution and Trigonometric/Algebraic Standard Forms
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{x\,dx}{(1+x)^2}\)
questions.explanation:
Substituting \(t=1+x\) gives \(x=t-1\), so \(\dfrac{x}{(1+x)^2}=\dfrac{1}{t}-\dfrac{1}{t^2}\), with antiderivative \(F=\log t+\dfrac{1}{t}\) in terms of \(t=1+x\).

At \(x=1\ (t=2)\): \(\log 2+\dfrac12\); at \(x=0\ (t=1)\): \(0+1\). Subtracting: \(\left(\log2+\dfrac12\right)-1 = \log2-\dfrac12\).
questions.hint: Substitute \(t=1+x\) to rewrite the numerator in terms of \(t\) before integrating.

Appends a constant of integration, which a definite integral's numeric value never carries
Introduces a sign error on the power term while substituting the upper limit

topics.name: Integration as the Inverse Process of Differentiation: Standard Integrals
topics.summary: Integration undoes differentiation: if \(\frac{d}{dx}F(x)=f(x)\), then \(\int f(x)\,dx=F(x)+C\). This topic covers the core list of standard integrals every other technique builds on — the power rule \(\int x^n dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\) (for \(n\neq -1\)), the basic trig integrals (\(\sin x,\cos x,\sec^2x,\operatorname{cosec}^2x\) and their products with \(\sec x,\operatorname{cosec}x\)), the exponential integral \(\int e^x dx=e^x+C\), and the four inverse-trig forms \(\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\) and \(\int\frac{dx}{1+x^2}\). Questions also test linearity (integrating term by term) and simple algebraic rearrangement — splitting a quotient into separate standard forms before integrating, or expanding a product first. The single most common way marks are lost here is forgetting the arbitrary constant \(C\) on an indefinite integral, or attaching one where it doesn't belong (on a definite integral's numeric answer). Mastering this list cold is the foundation for every harder integration technique that follows.
topics.worked_example: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int (x^2+1)^2\,dx\). Expand first: \((x^2+1)^2=x^4+2x^2+1\). Integrating term by term using the power rule: \(\int x^4dx+2\int x^2dx+\int 1\,dx = \dfrac{x^5}{5}+\dfrac{2x^3}{3}+x+C\).
common_mistakes: Dropping the constant \(C\) on an indefinite integral, or adding one to a definite integral's numeric value
Applying the power rule with \(n=-1\), where it fails and \(\log|x|\) must be used instead
Dividing by the original exponent instead of the new (incremented) exponent
Sign slips between \(\int\sin x\,dx\) and \(\int\cos x\,dx\)

topics.name: Integration by Substitution and Trigonometric/Algebraic Standard Forms
topics.summary: This topic covers integrals solved by substitution, along with a family of standard trigonometric and algebraic forms that recur constantly in exams. Substitution recognizes when an integrand contains a function together with (a multiple of) its own derivative, letting \(t=g(x)\) collapse the integral to a simple standard form. The standard forms include the four tangent-family integrals (\(\tan x,\cot x,\sec x,\operatorname{cosec}x\)), and — critically — four related-looking but distinct results: \(\int\frac{dx}{a^2-x^2}\) and \(\int\frac{dx}{x^2-a^2}\) (both logarithmic, with the sign inside the log flipped between them), versus \(\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}\) (arcsine) and \(\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}\) (log-of-sum). Completing the square converts quadratics like \(x^2+bx+c\) into one of these four standard shapes. The most exam-relevant skill is correctly matching a denominator's shape to the right one of these four formulas — mixing them up is one of the most common sources of lost marks in this chapter.
topics.worked_example: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{x^2-6x+13}\). Complete the square: \(x^2-6x+13=(x-3)^2+4\). This matches \(\int\frac{dx}{u^2+a^2}=\frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\frac{u}{a}+C\) with \(u=x-3,\ a=2\), giving \(\dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x-3}{2}+C\).
common_mistakes: Swapping which of \(a^2-x^2\) and \(x^2-a^2\) gets the arcsine form versus the log form
Flipping the sign inside the logarithm fraction
Forgetting to change the differential (and the limits, for definite integrals) after substituting
Completing the square incorrectly, leaving a mismatched constant term

topics.name: Integration by Partial Fractions
topics.summary: When the integrand is a rational function whose denominator factors, partial fractions rewrite it as a sum of simpler pieces that can each be integrated by a standard form. This topic covers denominators with distinct linear factors, at most one repeated linear factor, and at most one irreducible quadratic factor. For distinct linear factors \((x-a)(x-b)\), each contributes a term \(\frac{A}{x-a}\) that integrates to a logarithm. A repeated factor \((x-a)^2\) needs both \(\frac{A}{x-a}\) and \(\frac{B}{(x-a)^2}\) terms — the second integrates to a power, not a log. An irreducible quadratic factor needs a \(\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+\ldots}\) term, which splits into a logarithmic piece and an arctangent piece. When the numerator's degree is not less than the denominator's, always divide first — the setup only works on a proper fraction. Careful coefficient-matching and attention to which decomposition pattern a given denominator calls for are the key skills tested.
topics.worked_example: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{3x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\,dx\). Set \(\dfrac{3x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{x+2}\). Clearing denominators: \(A(x+2)+B(x-1)=3x+1\). Setting \(x=1\) gives \(A=\tfrac43\); setting \(x=-2\) gives \(B=\tfrac53\). Integrating: \(\dfrac{4}{3}\log|x-1|+\dfrac{5}{3}\log|x+2|+C\).
common_mistakes: Using only a single \(\frac{A}{x-a}\) term for a repeated linear factor instead of two terms
Forgetting the numerator \(Bx+C\) (not just a constant) for an irreducible quadratic factor
Skipping polynomial long division when the numerator's degree is not less than the denominator's
Mixing up which root goes with which coefficient when back-substituting to solve for \(A,B\)

topics.name: Integration by Parts
topics.summary: Integration by parts handles a product of two different types of function — typically a polynomial times a trig, exponential, or logarithmic factor — using \(\int u\,dv = uv-\int v\,du\). The ILATE rule (Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential) gives a rough priority order for choosing \(u\): pick the factor earlier in that list as \(u\) so it simplifies (or at least doesn't get worse) on differentiating, and the rest as \(dv\). When the polynomial factor has degree 2 or 3, by parts must be applied twice (or three times), each round reducing the polynomial's degree by one. Two special recurring patterns deserve separate recognition: the cyclic case (\(\int e^x\sin x\,dx\) or \(\int e^x\cos x\,dx\)), where applying by parts twice brings back the original integral, solved by treating it as an algebraic equation; and the pattern \(\int e^x[f(x)+f'(x)]\,dx=e^xf(x)+C\), which needs no computation at all once spotted. Choosing \(u\) and \(dv\) correctly, and tracking signs across repeated applications, are the main sources of error.
topics.worked_example: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int x^2e^{2x}\,dx\). With \(u=x^2,\ dv=e^{2x}dx\) (so \(v=\tfrac12e^{2x}\)): \(\int x^2e^{2x}dx = \dfrac{x^2e^{2x}}{2}-\int xe^{2x}\,dx\). Applying by parts again on \(\int xe^{2x}dx\) gives \(\dfrac{xe^{2x}}{2}-\dfrac{e^{2x}}{4}\), so the full answer is \(\dfrac{x^2e^{2x}}{2}-\dfrac{xe^{2x}}{2}+\dfrac{e^{2x}}{4}+C\).
common_mistakes: Choosing \(u\) and \(dv\) in the wrong order, making the leftover integral harder instead of simpler
Losing track of a chain-rule factor (like the 2 in \(e^{2x}\)) when finding \(v\) from \(dv\)
Sign errors accumulating across two or three rounds of by parts on a higher-degree polynomial
Failing to recognize the cyclic pattern and attempting to apply by parts indefinitely instead of solving algebraically

topics.name: Definite Integrals: Fundamental Theorem, Substitution, and Properties
topics.summary: A definite integral \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) is evaluated by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus as \(F(b)-F(a)\), where \(F\) is any antiderivative of \(f\) — the result is always a pure number, never carrying \(+C\). Substitution works the same way as for indefinite integrals, except the limits must also be converted to the new variable rather than substituted back at the end. Several properties streamline harder definite integrals: reversing limits flips the sign (\(\int_a^b=-\int_b^a\)); King's property \(\int_0^af(x)dx=\int_0^af(a-x)dx\) (or its general form \(\int_a^bf(x)dx=\int_a^bf(a+b-x)dx\)) is powerful when adding the original and transformed integrals produces a simpler combined integrand; odd functions integrate to zero over a symmetric interval, while even functions double the integral over the half-interval; and integrands involving a modulus, or otherwise changing formula partway through, must be split at the point where the behavior changes before integrating each piece separately. Recognizing which property applies — and not misapplying it — is the central skill.
topics.worked_example: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} \dfrac{x\,dx}{1+\sin x}\) using King's property with \(a=\pi\): letting \(I\) denote the integral, \(I=\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{(\pi-x)\,dx}{1+\sin x}\) (since \(\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x\)). Adding: \(2I=\pi\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{dx}{1+\sin x}\), which reduces (via the standard half-angle substitution) to a value that gives \(I\) directly.
common_mistakes: Attaching a \(+C\) to a definite integral's final numeric answer, or omitting a required \(+C\) on an indefinite one
Computing \(F(a)-F(b)\) instead of \(F(b)-F(a)\)
Substituting a new variable but forgetting to convert the limits of integration to match
Integrating straight through a modulus or piecewise sign change without splitting the interval first
